notes: Divisional Court appeals on R18 mail-order supply; statutory construction and Article 10 analysis are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Interfact and Pabo: R18 video mail order and Video Recordings Act supply
key_facts: Pabo and Interfact, licensed sex-shop operators, were convicted of supplying or offering to supply R18 videos by post and telephone to Liverpool trading standards test purchases.
The transactions were not completed with the customer physically present in the licensed sex shop.
The operators argued supply occurred in the shop when orders were accepted and dispatched, and that catalogues were invitations to treat rather than offers to supply.
Article 10 was invoked to argue that prohibiting mail order was a disproportionate interference with freedom of expression.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals by case stated from Liverpool Magistrates' Court convictions under section 12(1) of the Video Recordings Act 1984.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; supply and offer to supply R18 recordings other than in a licensed sex shop with the customer present were criminal offences; Article 10 did not require a different construction; a point of general public importance was certified.
enrichment.ratio: Supply under the Video Recordings Act means transfer of physical possession, not contractual acceptance in the shop; an offer to supply under section 12(1)(b) is an offer to make supply outside a licensed sex shop, not merely an offer made outside the shop; the restriction is necessary and proportionate under Article 10.2 for the protection of morals.
legal_issues: Whether mail or telephone supply of R18 videos from a licensed sex shop is supply other than in the shop
Whether catalogues amounted to offers to supply under section 12(1)(b)
Whether section 3 of the Human Rights Act required a narrower construction
Whether the Pabo costs order was wrong in the exercise of discretion
linked_authorities: Delgado [1984] 1 WLR 89
Maginnis [1987] 1 AC 303
Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza [2004] UKHL 30

notes: Short permission judgment on EAT extension of time; discretionary standard is clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: CFP v Bayley: permission to appeal out-of-time EAT refusal
key_facts: Miss Bayley succeeded in the Employment Tribunal on an unlawful deduction from wages claim for £10,122.13 against CFP Independent Advisers Ltd.
The company’s appeal notice was 71 days late after the Registrar refused an extension of the 42-day limit.
Judge Peter Clark dismissed the company’s appeal against the Registrar’s refusal, finding no good excuse for the delay.
Mr Campopiano, the company director, contended the underlying tribunal decision was unjust and that commission had never been received.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal’s refusal to extend time for appealing a tribunal award.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; no real prospect of success on an appeal against the exercise of discretion to refuse a long extension of time.
enrichment.ratio: An appeal against refusal to extend time for bringing an employment appeal is an appeal against discretion and will succeed only if the discretion was exercised through error of legal principle or is plainly wrong; disagreement with the underlying tribunal merits is not enough.
legal_issues: Whether the EAT erred in refusing a 71-day extension of time
Whether exceptional circumstances justified allowing a very late appeal
Whether the underlying tribunal decision on commission was relevant on a time-extension appeal

notes: Castor Group litigation; section 51 shareholder funder costs analysis is authoritative and detailed.

enrichment.short_title: CIBC Mellon v Stolzenberg: non-party shareholder costs after default judgments
key_facts: Claimants obtained very large default judgments against Mora and Chascona in Castor Group fraud proceedings after unless-order breaches.
Mr Cavazza, owning 75% of the companies, funded and directed unsuccessful applications to set aside the judgments.
Etherton J ordered Cavazza to pay set-aside costs but refused to order him to pay costs of detailed assessment of the 1999 judgment debts.
Detailed assessment costs exceeded £500,000 and set-aside costs were billed at about £1 million.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from orders under section 51 of the Supreme Court Act 1981 making a shareholder funder personally liable for costs.
enrichment.outcome: Cross-appeal dismissed; appeal allowed; Cavazza ordered to pay costs assessment costs and Court of Appeal costs from the set-aside refusal.
enrichment.ratio: A shareholder who is not a director may be ordered to pay costs where he funds, controls and directs litigation in the company’s name for his own financial interest; a funder who usurps directors’ role acts at his own risk, following Chapman and Fulton Motors; detailed assessment after set-aside applications was justifiable and necessary once those applications were made.
legal_issues: Whether a shareholder funder may be liable for company litigation costs absent bad faith
Whether the judge erred in refusing costs assessment costs against Cavazza
Distinction between Metalloy and Fulton Motors on director-funded litigation
Whether security-for-costs failure precluded a section 51 order
linked_authorities: Chapman v Christopher [1998] 1 WLR 12
Metalloy Supplies Ltd v MA (UK) Ltd [1997] 1 WLR 1613
Fulton Motors Ltd v Toyota (GB) Ltd (23 July 1999)

notes: Guarantee scope on loan replacement appeal; variation and estoppel analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Triodos v Dobbs: guarantee scope after replacement loan facilities
key_facts: Mr Dobbs gave a £50,000 personal guarantee of Acorn Televillages Ltd’s liabilities under 1996 loan agreements totalling £900,000 for a Crickhowell televillage project.
The bank replaced those loans with larger 1998 agreements and a 1999 facility of up to £2.6 million, each expressly retaining the 1996 guarantee as security.
After receivership and sale of the site, the bank claimed the shortfall from Dobbs under the 1996 guarantee.
The judge granted summary judgment and held Dobbs estopped by convention from denying the guarantee covered later borrowing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from summary judgment declarations that the 1996 guarantee extended to the 1999 facility and that Dobbs was estopped.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; declarations set aside; guarantee did not cover substantially different 1999 facility; estoppel by convention could not be decided summarily.
enrichment.ratio: A guarantee of sums due under or pursuant to specified loan agreements does not extend to liabilities under a later replacement facility that is materially beyond amendment or variation within the purview of the original agreement; rescheduling contemplated by the original agreement may be covered, but tripling borrowing for new works is not; estoppel by convention requires a common assumption of fact, which could not be found summarily against Dobbs’s evidence.
legal_issues: Construction of guarantee clause 2.4.1 permitting amendments without guarantor consent
Whether 1998 and 1999 facilities were variations within the original guarantee
Material variation discharging a surety
Estoppel by convention on summary judgment
linked_authorities: Trade Indemnity Co Ltd v Workington Harbour and Dock Board [1937] AC 1
British Motor Trust Co Ltd v Hyams (1934) 50 TLR 230
Samuels Finance Group Plc v Beechmanor Ltd [1993] P&CR 282

notes: Anticipatory breach and Part 36 costs on split trial; Waller LJ’s CPR analysis is instructive.

enrichment.short_title: HSS v BMB: anticipatory breach of tool-hire licence and Part 36 costs
key_facts: HSS operated a tool-hire agency under a five-year licence in BMB branches; change of control of BMB to Grafton was an event of default unless agreed.
After Grafton confirmed it would not continue the agency, HSS arranged to collect materials and treated BMB as repudiating; BMB later wrote suggesting mutual termination.
The judge found anticipatory repudiatory breach by BMB on 23 May 2002 and wrongful interference by Grafton.
BMB sought permission to appeal and challenged a costs order made after a split trial despite a Part 36 payment in.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal with immediate appeal granted on costs; challenge to liability findings and Part 36 costs after preliminary issue trial.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal liability refused; permission granted on costs; costs order reversed so costs of liability issue reserved pending damages assessment.
enrichment.ratio: BMB’s conduct after Grafton’s refusal amounted to an anticipatory repudiatory breach accepted by HSS; the case was decided on pleaded facts without needing agency of Grafton’s director; where liability is determined before quantum and a Part 36 payment has been made, costs of the preliminary issue should normally be reserved until all issues are resolved.
legal_issues: Whether conversations on 23 May 2002 constituted anticipatory repudiatory breach
Whether the case was decided on an unpleaded basis
Effect of Part 36 payment when costs of split trial are awarded
Tortious interference with contract by Grafton
linked_authorities: Beaco Ltd v Alfa Laval Ltd [1995] QB 137

notes: Landmark section 44(3) construction on urgent arbitral injunctions; Hiscox distinguished.

enrichment.short_title: Cetelem v Roust: section 44 urgent mandatory injunction in arbitration
key_facts: Cetelem agreed to buy a 50% interest in a Cypriot company under an English-law SPA with ICC arbitration, conditional on Russian Central Bank approval by 31 January 2005.
Without arbitral proceedings commenced, Cetelem obtained without-notice freezing and mandatory orders requiring RHL to deliver documents for the Central Bank application.
Beatson J continued the orders; RHL challenged jurisdiction under section 44(3) as going beyond preserving evidence or assets.
The share-purchase right was argued to be an asset that the mandatory order preserved pending arbitration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal against interim mandatory and freezing orders under section 44 of the Arbitration Act 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to appeal granted on jurisdiction but appeal dismissed; section 44(3) in urgent cases is limited to orders necessary to preserve evidence or assets, but the mandatory order fell within that power; section 44(7) permits appeal where the judge lacked jurisdiction on the wider basis used.
enrichment.ratio: In urgent cases section 44(3) does not confer unrestricted section 44(1) powers but only orders the court thinks necessary to preserve evidence or assets, contrary to Hiscox; a contractual right to purchase shares is an asset for this purpose; a decision made without jurisdiction is not a decision under the section for section 44(7) appeal purposes.
legal_issues: Construction of section 44(3) versus sections 44(4) and (5)
Whether mandatory performance orders usurp the arbitral tribunal
Whether contractual rights are assets under section 44(3)
Jurisdiction to appeal despite section 44(7) leave requirement

notes: SENDIST school placement appeal; Makaton-focused Wednesbury review is careful and fact-specific.

enrichment.short_title: Southwark v SENDIST: autistic child’s school placement and Makaton
key_facts: Daniel Oyedipe, a severely autistic almost-seven-year-old, challenged parts 3 and 4 of his statement of special educational needs.
Southwark named Cherry Garden School; his parents sought The Rainbow School, an independent autistic-specific school using Makaton throughout.
Daniel communicated mainly through about 60 Makaton signs after a home-based ABA programme; Cherry Garden emphasised PECS with limited Makaton.
The Secretary of State consented under section 347(5)(b) to placement at the unapproved Rainbow School.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal on a point of law from SENDIST upholding the parents’ choice of school in part 4 of the statement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Tribunal’s choice of Rainbow School was not unsupported by evidence or Wednesbury unreasonable.
enrichment.ratio: On a SENDIST appeal the court may interfere only on questions of law; Makaton integration was a material issue on the evidence and the Tribunal was entitled to prefer Rainbow School where Makaton was used routinely by staff and peers; DFES registration and other LEAs’ funding provided limited reassurance but were not decisive of suitability for Daniel.
legal_issues: Whether there was sufficient evidence that Rainbow School could meet Daniel’s SEN
Whether the Tribunal took irrelevant account of DFES approval and other LEA placements
Whether Makaton use at each school was adequately found
Whether failure to find Cherry Garden teacher’s Makaton training was material

notes: Article 3 suicide-risk immigration appeal; foreign/domestic distinction carefully analysed.

enrichment.short_title: J v SSHD: Article 3 and suicide risk on removal to Sri Lanka
key_facts: A Sri Lankan Tamil with PTSD and depression claimed he would commit suicide if removed after torture by the army and detention by the LTTE.
Psychiatric evidence reported prior overdose, ongoing suicidal ideation and high risk on final removal decision.
The adjudicator and IAT rejected asylum and human rights claims, finding family and medical support would manage risk in the UK and Sri Lanka.
Objective risk of persecution on return was not established.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Immigration Appeal Tribunal dismissal of a human rights appeal based on articles 3 and 8.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no real risk of article 3 breach from suicide in the UK, in transit or in Sri Lanka on the evidence.
enrichment.ratio: In removal cases the article 3 test differs between domestic stages (risk in the UK) and foreign stages (real risk in the receiving state); suicide risk can engage article 3 but requires severity, causation and regard to protective mechanisms; where fears of ill-treatment abroad are unfounded and UK mental health and escort arrangements exist, the high article 3 threshold is not met.
legal_issues: Correct test for article 3 where removal may cause suicide
Distinction between foreign and domestic cases after Ullah
Whether IAT erred in rejecting psychiatric evidence on UK suicide risk
Risk of suicide en route and on arrival in Sri Lanka
linked_authorities: Ullah v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] UKHL 26
Soumahoro v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWCA Civ 840
Bensaid v United Kingdom (2001) 33 EHRR 10

notes: Discontinuance of fraud claim against impecunious defendant; Walker v Walker costs principles applied.

enrichment.short_title: RBG Resources v Patel: discontinuance costs after fraud allegations
key_facts: Liquidators sued Mr Patel alleging involvement in a massive metals-trading fraud that caused RBG’s insolvent liquidation; summary judgment was obtained against directors but not Patel.
Freezing and restraint orders were obtained in 2002; Laddie J held there was a good arguable fraud case and refused to set aside the freezing order.
Patel insisted on public exoneration and indemnity costs as a condition of settlement; the claimant lacked funds to proceed to trial.
The claimant applied to discontinue with no order as to costs; Patel sought indemnity costs and enforcement of cross-undertakings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to discontinue fraud claim and for costs and cross-undertaking relief under CPR Part 38.
enrichment.outcome: Discontinuance permitted on terms that the claimant pay 60% of Patel’s costs on the standard basis; no indemnity costs; restraint order costs and cross-undertaking claim refused.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR 38.6 the default on discontinuance is that the claimant pays the defendant’s costs unless there is good reason to depart; pursuing an impecunious defendant until funds are exhausted then discontinuing does not avoid that rule; unreasonable refusal to settle without exoneration can justify reducing costs awarded, following Walker v Walker.
legal_issues: Terms on which discontinuance should be permitted where fraud is alleged
Whether Walker v Walker requires indemnity costs
Costs of section 236 restraint proceedings
Cross-undertaking damages for spread-betting losses under freezing order
linked_authorities: Walker v Walker [2005] EWCA Civ 247

notes: Extension of vexatious litigant injunction against Ebert; Divisional Court control measures are comprehensive.

enrichment.short_title: Attorney-General v Ebert: extension of vexatious litigant restrictions
key_facts: Mr Ebert had been subject since 2001 to an injunction restricting court access and requiring written applications after a section 42 civil proceedings order over Europride-related litigation.
Despite the orders he made hundreds of further applications challenging his 1997 bankruptcy and related matters, and sent abusive correspondence to judges and court staff.
A criminal proceedings section 42 order was also made in 2004.
The Attorney-General sought indefinite extension of the 2001 injunction and a bar on further bankruptcy-related applications.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Divisional Court application by the Attorney-General to extend and widen injunctive relief against a vexatious litigant.
enrichment.outcome: Injunction extended without limit of time; Ebert restrained from abusive communications and from section 42 applications on bankruptcy and Europride matters; future applications rationed to twice yearly; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Courts may restrict access to protect their processes from persistent vexatious relitigation of finally decided matters; abusive correspondence with judges and staff may be restrained; Article 6 does not prevent proportionate limits on a litigant who has exhausted merit in repeated applications; Freedom of Information requests made to reopen closed litigation may be vexatious under section 14.
legal_issues: Whether the 2001 injunction should be extended and made permanent
Whether Ebert should be barred from bankruptcy-related section 42 applications
Compatibility with Article 6 and fundamental rights
Restraint of abusive correspondence with the court
linked_authorities: Attorney-General v Ebert [2001] EWHC Admin 695
Attorney-General v Jones [1990] 1 WLR 859
Mahajan v Waldman [2003] EWCA Civ 1899
